cards.title: Model Amazon FBA unit economics with the three-big-fees framework
cards.summary: Split every candidate product's selling price into product cost, Amazon fees and profit using a thirds rule before committing to inventory.
cards.use_when: Pricing and product selection: deciding whether a product can survive Amazon's fee stack, or setting a target retail price.
steps: List the three big fees: the referral fee (a flat percentage to sell on Amazon; the source uses 15%), the FBA pick-and-pack fee (per unit, based on size and weight), and the monthly storage fee (charged per cubic foot of warehouse space).
Sanity-check the split the source uses as a planning rule of thumb: roughly 33% of margin to product cost, 33% to Amazon FBA fees, 33% profit. Treat it as a heuristic, not a calculation.

Plug a real comparable product's price, dimensions and weight into Amazon's free FBA calculator to get referral fee, pick-and-pack fee and monthly storage cost per unit. Verify the current calculator's interface and current fee tables before relying on output.
Compare the resulting per-unit contribution against your target profit, and reject products where fee load pushes you below target before you spend on design, samples or inventory.
Re-check numbers for the apparel category (roughly $0.30-$0.40 more per shipped item per the source) and for dangerous goods, which bill at different tiers.
caveats: The 33/33/33 split is the presenter's rule of thumb, not a derived formula; actual results vary widely by price point and size.
Fee amounts and thresholds change; the numbers cited are examples from the source's experience and date, so confirm current Amazon fee schedules.

cards.title: Choose small-standard packaging deliberately to cut pick-and-pack fees
cards.summary: Design product dimensions and weight to land in the cheapest FBA size tier, since pick-and-pack pricing moves sharply by tier and weight band.
cards.use_when: Product and packaging design or sourcing: specifying box dimensions, jar size, or bundle configuration before ordering inventory.
steps: Apply the source's stated tier boundaries: small standard means longest side up to 15 in, median side up to 12 in, shortest side up to 0.75 in, and weight under 1 lb. Large standard means up to 18 in longest, 14 in median, 8 in shortest, and under 20 lb. Verify the current Amazon definitions, which do change.

Within a tier, weight bands drive the fee: the source cites different fees for under 6 oz, 6-12 oz, and 12-16 oz for small standard. Shaving a product just under a band boundary can reduce cost per unit.

Give the manufacturer a target spec rather than accepting their default. The source's example: instead of a 16 oz jar, he produced a smaller jar under 10 oz specifically to lower FBA pick-and-pack fees.

For low-price, lightweight products, check whether the product qualifies for Amazon's Small and Light program; the source cites an example of $2.16 per unit instead of $2.70, a $0.54 per-unit saving, and reports that a colleague saved hundreds to thousands of dollars.

After your first shipments, verify Amazon recorded the correct dimensions and weight; the source says Amazon sometimes places products in a higher tier and will sometimes reimburse overcharges if you catch it and contact them.
caveats: Tier dimensions, weight bands, and program fees are set by Amazon and change; re-verify before tooling packaging.
Making the product smaller can reduce perceived value or change the use case, so weigh fee savings against customer expectations.

cards.title: Estimate monthly storage cost and avoid long-term storage fees
cards.summary: Calculate per-unit storage cost from cubic volume and plan inventory turnover so units don't sit in Amazon warehouses past 365 days.
cards.use_when: Replenishment and inventory planning: deciding how many units to send to FBA and when to pull slow stock.
steps: Measure product height, width and depth to get cubic inches. Divide by 1,728 (cubic inches in a cubic foot) and multiply by the per-cubic-foot rate. The source's example: a 3x4x5 in product is 60 cubic in, giving about $0.026 per unit per month at $0.75/cubic foot.

Account for the seasonal rate: the source cites roughly $0.70 per cubic foot January-September and $2.40 per cubic foot October-December, because Amazon raises fees to discourage Q4 overstocking. Confirm current rates.
Estimate total storage by multiplying per-unit monthly cost by the months you expect the unit to remain in the warehouse, and fold that into your unit economics.
Avoid the long-term storage fee: if inventory stays past 365 days, the source says Amazon charges $6.90 per cubic foot or $0.15 per item, whichever is greater.
Monitor sell-through. If a SKU is slow, request removal before the one-year mark, even if you intend to re-ship it back in, or let it sell down and reset the clock with fresh inventory.

Size shipments so you don't end up with residual units sitting past a year: the source contrasts 100 units selling 50/month (clock resets continually) with 100 units selling 10/month (20 units remain after 12 months and start accruing long-term fees).
caveats: Rates are cited from the source's experience and change; verify current Amazon storage fee schedules.
Removal and re-shipment costs can rival the long-term storage fee for very cheap, very small items.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Decide FBA vs FBM based on Prime eligibility and rank impact
cards.summary: Use FBA when Prime eligibility and search ranking matter more than per-unit fulfillment savings, reserving FBM for cases where it genuinely fits.
cards.use_when: Fulfillment model choice for a new listing, or deciding whether to migrate seller-fulfilled SKUs into FBA.
steps: Recognize what FBA buys you: Prime eligibility (two-day delivery), higher search ranking, and no per-order packing or post-office trips. FBM means you pick, pack and ship every order yourself.

Weigh the switch against your own data. The source reports that after moving products from seller-fulfilled to FBA, sales increased four to five times. Treat this as one seller's result, not a benchmark.
Budget for the pick-and-pack fee as the price of that upgrade, and model it into unit economics before migrating.

Consider FBM only where FBA fees or restrictions genuinely make it uneconomic (for example, unusual size or direct-ship arrangements), and accept the fulfillment labor and slower delivery as the trade.
Keep the professional selling plan in place for FBA, since the source says you need it to send inventory into Amazon's warehouses.
caveats: The 4-5x sales lift is one seller's before/after observation and is not a promised outcome.
FBA ties up inventory in Amazon warehouses, creating long-term storage and removal exposure if the product stalls.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Pick the right Amazon selling plan instead of paying monthly from day one
cards.summary: Match the individual vs professional selling plan to actual monthly order volume to avoid paying $39.99/month before you're selling.
cards.use_when: Pre-launch account setup and cost control while sourcing a product or running low-volume arbitrage.
steps: Use the individual selling plan while you're not yet live or selling few units: the source describes it as free to hold, with a $0.99 fee per item sold, and recommends it below roughly 40 items per month.

Upgrade to the professional plan at $39.99/month when volume crosses that band or when you're ready to send inventory to FBA, since the source says FBA requires the professional plan and gives access to promotions and reports.
Avoid the common mistake the source flags: paying $39.99/month for months while still only thinking about starting, before any inventory is sent in.
Treat the ~40 items/month crossover as the source's heuristic and recalculate with your own average selling price and per-item fee.
caveats: The break-even item count depends on per-item fee and current plan pricing; verify current Amazon selling plan terms.
Feature availability on each plan can change.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Reduce the referral fee from 15% to 5% by driving your own traffic
cards.summary: Use the brand referral bonus program so sales from traffic you generate yourself are billed at a lower referral rate.
cards.use_when: Acquisition and off-Amazon marketing: running ads, influencer or social traffic to your own Amazon listing.
steps: Confirm you're eligible and enrolled in Amazon's brand referral bonus program, which the source says requires brand registry and provides a special link for tracking traffic you send.
Generate the tracking link inside the program and use it in your off-Amazon campaigns (ads, email, social) so Amazon attributes the visit to you.
Expect the standard referral fee (the source cites 15%) to drop to about 5% on attributed sales, and calculate the incremental margin into your ad budget so you can bid more aggressively.

Compare the outcome against sending that same traffic to your own website: the source argues conversion is much higher on Amazon because of built-in trust, which is why he considers the 5% well spent.
Track attributed sales separately so you can see the real blended referral rate.
caveats: Program name, rate, and eligibility rules are Amazon-controlled and have changed over time; verify current terms before planning margins around it.
The claim that Amazon converts better than your own site is the presenter's opinion, not a measured comparison.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Cut avoidable FBA prep, return and disposal fees
cards.summary: Handle labeling and prep yourself or through your manufacturer to avoid per-unit Amazon service charges, and plan for returns and disposal costs.
cards.use_when: Sourcing, packaging and post-sale operations: negotiating labeling with your manufacturer and setting up returns handling.
steps: Ensure every unit carries an FNSKU barcode sticker before it reaches Amazon. Have your manufacturer apply stickers cheaply or print the barcode directly on the box, rather than paying Amazon the source's cited $0.30 per unit labeling fee.

Handle any other prep (poly bagging, etc.) yourself or at the factory; the source says Amazon charges about $0.50-$2.00 per unit for these services. Read the prep requirements for your specific category.
Budget for return fees: the source says each customer return within 30 days triggers another size/weight-based fee covering return shipping and processing.
Choose what happens to returned units: have Amazon return good-condition units to your sellable inventory so the next order ships that same unit, or have them disposed of at roughly $0.50 per unit.
Optionally review undeliverable inventory and remove it rather than letting it accrue fees.
caveats: Prep service and disposal fees, and category prep requirements, change; confirm current rates and rules.
The source describes return and disposal fees as relatively small and uncommon, but they matter more for high-return categories like apparel.

cards.title: Budget a private-label launch from a component checklist
cards.summary: Build a line-item startup budget covering plan fee, design, samples, inventory, photos, business registration, UPCs and cushion before committing.
cards.use_when: Launch budgeting for a private-label or wholesale product, or deciding whether you have enough capital to start.
steps: Include the recurring professional selling plan ($39.99/month per the source) and confirm whether you need it for your fulfillment model.

Budget design: the source recommends hiring a legitimate designer and cites about $150 for a private-label logo and label, advising against relying on the cheapest Fiverr option for brand-critical work.
Budget samples: the source cites about $50 shipping per sample round and recommends at least one sample, ideally two, to catch defects before mass production.

Budget first inventory around 400 units at roughly $6/unit (about $2,400) as his default illustration, and check whether your unit cost drops at higher volumes (the source cites ~$5.50 at 1,000 units and ~$5 at 2,000 units).
Budget photography: the source says the main image drives clicks and purchases and recommends $50-$100 for a computer rendering, treating the other listing images as doable in-house.

Add business registration ($150 DBA via LegalZoom, or ~$350 LLC setup plus recurring state fees such as California's $800/year), GS1 UPC codes (~$250 for 10), and about $100 of miscellaneous costs (sticker paper, ink, gas).
Add a marketing reserve: the source suggests at least $1,000 for Amazon PPC and argues that under about $5,000 total, he would advise against starting at all.
caveats: All figures are the presenter's planning estimates from his own launches, not vendor quotes or guarantees.
He explicitly says the $3,500 minimum assumes everything goes perfectly and no marketing is needed, which he calls unrealistic; the $5,000 figure is his recommended realistic floor.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Order 3-6 months of inventory, not the cheapest per-unit quantity
cards.summary: Size your first production run for 3-6 months of expected sales rather than chase volume discounts that lock up cash in unproven product.
cards.use_when: Replenishment and first production order: choosing quantity with a manufacturer before you have sales data.
steps: Estimate expected monthly unit sales and order enough for 3-6 months, favoring the higher end because manufacturer lead times mean you can't restock quickly if sales spike.

Weigh the volume discount against the risk. The source's case study: ordering 2,000 units at ~$5/unit cost $11,000, versus 400 units at ~$7/unit costing about $2,800; he calls the large order a mistake because it took far longer to sell than expected and locked in early product defects.
Avoid running out: the source warns that stockouts can cause Amazon to penalize the listing and make it hard to regain sales velocity, which is his reason for leaning toward the 6-month end.
Order a small test batch first when the product is new or has known issues, fix defects, then scale quantity.
Account for landed cost beyond unit price: the source mentions import duties (he recalls 10%, possibly 20%) that vary by product, so check current rates rather than assuming.
caveats: The lead-time and stockout penalty arguments are the presenter's experience and may not apply to easily restockable domestic suppliers.
Shelf-stable products can justify larger runs than perishables or trend-sensitive goods.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Register a trademark as a design mark to unlock Brand Registry
cards.summary: File a logo design mark rather than a word mark to boost approval odds and gain Brand Registry tools like enhanced brand content.
cards.use_when: Brand protection and listing presentation for a private-label product that needs richer PDP content and defense against hijackers.
steps: Decide whether Brand Registry benefits justify the cost: the source cites about $225 to file and lists protections against other sellers altering your listing or selling your product, plus A+ content (images, formatted text) and video on the product page.

File a design mark (your logo) rather than a word mark (your brand name): the source argues logos are easier to get approved because names are often generic — his examples are brands named as an adjective-plus-product and a name that's just a foreign word for the product.
File directly through the USPTO rather than paying roughly $1,000 for a trademark lawyer, per the source.

Treat trademarks as a listing-tooling investment rather than a litigation weapon: the source says enforcing or defending one costs tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars, so big-company enforcement battles aren't a realistic small-seller play.
caveats: The source's guidance is based on his own filings and conversations; trademark rules, fees and examination practice change.
Brand Registry benefits are Amazon-controlled and evolve.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Set an advertising budget from per-click cost, conversion rate and margin
cards.summary: Work backward from your per-sale margin to decide a viable cost per click, then treat PPC and product giveaways as launch-ranking costs.
cards.use_when: Product launch and acquisition planning: deciding how much to spend on Amazon PPC and how to interpret early ad spend.
steps: Estimate your cost per sale: if one in five clicks converts and you pay $1 per click, you're paying about $5 per sale. Substitute your own conversion rate once you have data.
Compare that cost per sale against your per-unit profit. The source's example: a $10 profit per sale against $5 ad cost leaves $5 — clearly worth continuing.
Set an initial budget rather than expecting organic sales: the source suggests at least $1,000 for PPC and says ranking a private-label product without ad spend is very hard.

Consider review-building tactics as an alternative launch lever. The source describes giveaway/coupon approaches and reimbursing friends for purchases plus reviews, while noting that reimbursing friends is technically against Amazon's rules even though he considers it hard for Amazon to detect — treat the compliant giveaway/coupon path as the primary option and check current Amazon review policies.
Reassess PPC efficiency after launch once you have real conversion and cost-per-click data instead of the illustrative numbers.
caveats: Conversion and cost-per-click figures in the source are hypothetical illustrations, not benchmarks.
Paid-review tactics violate Amazon policy; the presenter acknowledges this himself. Review policies are enforced and change.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Treat private label and wholesale as saturated, and differentiate instead
cards.summary: Evaluate private label/wholesale against structural headwinds and consider a novel own product to avoid price wars and Amazon's own copycats.
cards.use_when: Business model and product selection: choosing what to sell on Amazon before committing capital.
steps: Weigh four risks the source raises against private label and wholesale: Chinese manufacturers selling direct to Amazon and cutting out the middleman; similar disintermediation in wholesale; oversaturation (the source cites 5 million sellers and ~4,000 new sellers daily, driving price wars and margin erosion); and Amazon copying winning products with its own basics line that outranks you.

Note his observation that the consistently successful private-label and wholesale sellers tend to be long-established operators with more capital, tolerance for thin margins, and better manufacturer relationships than a newcomer.

Consider creating a product that doesn't yet exist as the alternative. The source's example is a set of wine flashcards — not revolutionary, but with no direct competitors, which he argues raises the odds customers buy.
Design for something you're genuinely interested in, since the source argues passion makes the long launch grind more survivable.
Consider crowdfunding to fund the first production run: the source raised about $15,000 on Kickstarter and cites a friend raising about $5,000, which can cover most or all startup costs.
caveats: These are the presenter's opinions and cited market observations, not measured research; private label and wholesale still work for some sellers, as he acknowledges.
Crowdfunding results vary enormously and require their own marketing effort.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Fund a launch without capital: sell assets, arbitrage and skill-building work
cards.summary: Raise initial capital by liquidating unused items, flipping discounted goods, cutting personal costs, and taking work that teaches Amazon skills.
cards.use_when: Launch funding and pre-launch skill building when you don't have savings to cover inventory and fees.
steps: Sell unused possessions you own but don't use (the source's examples: a surfboard and a hammock, about $100 each) to generate seed cash.

Run retail or online arbitrage: buy a product at a deep discount and resell on Amazon. The source's example is a $300 coffee machine bought for $150, netting roughly $100 after Amazon fees — useful for building cash and learning listing mechanics, though arbitrage margins are thin.
Reduce personal costs temporarily (cheaper housing, less premium food) and redirect the difference into inventory, as the source describes doing when starting out.

Take a second job that builds Amazon-relevant skills rather than unrelated work: the source suggests approaching local shops that sell unique products but aren't on Amazon and offering to list and sell for them for a fee or a profit share, which pays you while you learn.

Alternatively, find an investor for your product: the source's example is funding a friend's wine-flashcard business, recouping his money, and sharing in roughly $15-$20 profit per unit on 50-100 units sold monthly.
caveats: Arbitrage margins are thin and depend on finding genuine discounts; the source's example is illustrative.
The profit-share and investor examples are one-off case studies, not typical returns.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Pick a research tool: Helium 10 vs Jungle Scout
cards.summary: Choose a research tool based on filtering depth and data accuracy, with the source favoring Helium 10 for beginners.
cards.use_when: Product research and keyword/competitor analysis tooling decisions for an Amazon listing.
steps: Consider Helium 10 first if you want more tools, deeper filtering and, per the source, more accurate data — he recommends it for beginners and says it has way more tools than Jungle Scout.

Consider Jungle Scout as a valid alternative; the source explicitly says there's nothing wrong with it and calls it a great tool, so choose based on the specific filters and reports you'll actually use.
Check for discount links or affiliate offers associated with whichever tool you pick, since the source mentions providing a discounted rate.
Verify current pricing, tool set and data coverage directly with the vendor before subscribing, since both products change frequently.
caveats: This is the presenter's tool preference and may be influenced by affiliate relationships; validate with your own trials on products you know.
Tool feature sets and data accuracy change over time.
